summary: Describes an architecture for providing integrated services over low-bitrate links such as modems, ISDN B-channels and sub-T1 links. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2689 describes ways to support real-time traffic and integrated services over low-bitrate links. It combines link framing that reduces delay with header compression and information that helps systems negotiate how to handle each flow.

questions: how to reduce delay on slow links
how can real-time traffic use low-bitrate links
why use header compression for voice
subtitle: An architecture for real-time traffic and integrated services over low-bitrate links.

tldr.problem: Large packets can block time-sensitive traffic on low-bitrate links, while protocol headers can consume much of the bandwidth available to small real-time packets.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture combines real-time link encapsulation, header compression, application announcements and negotiation between peers and routers.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo describes an architecture, not a single protocol; it calls for coordination between encapsulation, compression and reservation mechanisms.

facts.label: Transmission time example
facts.value: About 400 milliseconds for a 1500-byte packet at 28.8 kbit/s

Compressed IP/UDP/RTP header
facts.value: As low as 2 bytes per packet

today: RFC 2689 is an Informational memo published in September 1999, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an architecture for providing integrated services over low-bitrate links.

sections.title: The Low-Bitrate Link Problem
sections.content:
The memo addresses integrated services for real-time multimedia over links such as modem lines, ISDN B-channels and sub-T1 links. A 1500-byte packet sent over a 28.8 kbit/s modem link occupies the link for about 400 milliseconds, delaying real-time packets that arrive while it is being sent.

Headers also consume a large share of a small packet. The memo gives at least 44 bytes of HDLC/PPP, IP, UDP and RTP overhead, compared with a 19.75-byte G.723.1 ACELP audio frame. Its design goals are to reduce worst-case delay, reduce protocol overhead and give admission control enough information about the flow's actual link use.
sections.plainLanguage: On a slow link, a large packet can delay real-time data waiting to be sent. Protocol headers also take up bandwidth that could otherwise carry the audio or video.

sections.title: Real-Time Encapsulation
sections.content:
Real-time encapsulation lets a sender introduce a time-sensitive packet before a long data packet has finished. The sender must be able to abort or suspend the long transfer and resume it later, so the link can serve a real-time flow without waiting for the entire packet.

The memo describes two sender models. A sender with byte-level control can suspend a packet when a higher-priority packet arrives. A sender that hands complete frames to its hardware cannot interrupt one, so it divides long packets into fragments small enough to meet its access-delay goals. The memo discusses link-layer framing and cites separate PPP specifications for multi-class and real-time-oriented HDLC-like framing.
sections.plainLanguage: Encapsulation should let a time-sensitive packet interrupt a long transfer and then let that transfer continue. Hardware that cannot pause a frame can instead divide long packets into smaller pieces.

sections.title: Compressing Headers
sections.content:
Real-time encapsulation does not remove the header overhead of HDLC/PPP, IP, UDP and RTP. The memo describes header compression as a way for the two ends of a link to share state: after information has been established, the sender can omit repeated fields and the receiver can reconstruct them.

The cited IP header compression can reduce a 28-byte IPv4/UDP header to about 6 bytes, depending on the number of streams. Compression of RTP sequence numbers and timestamps can use their predictable changes. The memo says the combined IP/UDP/RTP header can be reduced to two bytes per packet in the described techniques, and notes that this compression need only be used at bottleneck links.
sections.plainLanguage: Header compression avoids sending fields that stay the same or change predictably. The receiver uses shared information to rebuild them, leaving more link capacity for the real-time data.

sections.title: Announcing Flows and Negotiating Settings
sections.content:
Compression works best when systems can identify a real-time flow and know its payload format. The memo notes that RSVP PATH messages already carry traffic specifications, and proposes that additional RSVP objects could describe information useful for low-bitrate links. Routers that do not need those objects could ignore them.

Peer routers or hosts can negotiate which flows to compress, which header fields to omit, what multiplexing information to use and how to encode remaining fields. PPP link setup is presented as a suitable place to negotiate real-time encapsulation and compression options.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can announce what kind of flow they will send, and peer systems can negotiate how to carry it. This lets them agree on compression and encapsulation settings before using them.

sections.title: Security and Compression Assumptions
sections.content:
Header-compression techniques that rely on assumptions about application protocols need careful analysis. If a compressor applies those assumptions to the wrong traffic, it may reconstruct packets incorrectly and disrupt another application.

The memo says substantial hop-by-hop compression is generally not possible on encrypted streams because the compressor cannot inspect the headers. Depending on security policy, systems may compress decapsulated packets at a network access server before sending them over an encrypted link, or use a payload format that encrypts data without encrypting headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression must identify the right traffic and use assumptions that match its protocol. Encryption can hide fields a compressor needs, so compression and security arrangements must be coordinated.
